newsitem.title: UK: High-scoring dollar pares gains in late Europe.
newsitem.headline: High-scoring dollar pares gains in late Europe.

text.p: The dollar sprinted to a six-year peak against the mark after the Bundesbank left monetary policy unchanged, but a profit-taking wave and swings in the Swiss franc eroded much of those gains in late Europe.
The U.S. unit soared to a high of 1.8400 earlier as players expressed relief that the German central bank had not switched from a fixed to a variable repo rate as some had speculated.
"The reaction to the Bundesbank leaving things steady was to take the dollar up," said Graham Cocks, vice-president, treasury at Bank of Boston in London.

But the Bundesbank -- after its last council meeting before the four-week summer break -- kept alive market fears of higher rates. It said the repo would be held at its current 3.0 percent for at least the next two weeks but made no comment on where the rate would be during the second half of the recess.
"They seem to be holding out the threat of a tightening, which could be mark-positive in the days ahead," said Ian Morris, international economist at HSBC James Capel here.
The dollar retreated from its 1.84 marks high to 1.8288/98 by 1528 GMT, though it remained above late Wednesday's European level of 1.8240/50.
Traders said Swiss franc movements had exerted a big pull on dollar/mark in afternoon Europe.
An unusually volatile mark/Swiss slid to an 11-month low of 80.90 centimes, only to bounce sharply to 81.92/94 by 1553 GMT, well up from late Wednesday's 81.28/38.
Dollar/Swiss scored a 43-month high of 1.5033 francs as mark/Swiss slumped, before backtracking to 1.4990/00. It closed here at 1.4840/50 yesterday.
Traders said stop-loss orders were triggered on the break above 1.4922, the former 1997 high. Failed attempts to defend a sizeable options play with a 1.49 strike also helped, they said.
Dollar/yen was again sidelined, trading at 115.84/94 at 1557 GMT compared to late yesterday's 115.73/78.

The dollar shrugged off a bigger than expected fall in U.S. weekly jobless claims to 299,000 from 341,000 the previous week. Friday sees the release of June U.S. durable goods orders, expected to rise 1.4 percent after a 0.6 drop last time.

The soaring mark/Swiss rate hauled the German unit up on most of its European crosses in late trade. But analysts said some correction was inevitable after the mark's recent hammering, and said the bigger picture still looked bleak for the mark.

"As long as EMU's going ahead, as long as the market's discounting that...and if Italian first-wave membership of EMU becomes more likely, you could see the mark trading at 2.0 against the dollar," said Capel's Morris.
The growing conviction that monetary union will be launched on time by a broad range of countries -- making for a soft, inflation-prone euro -- has taken a heavy toll on the mark.
With the market stubbornly in that frame of mind, it paid little heed to the Bundesbank's warning today that it would keep a close eye on developments in the financial markets.

Traders and analysts said verbal intervention cut little ice with the market at present, and even physical central bank action -- judged increasingly unlikely -- would probably do little to turn back the dollar-bullish tide.
Even the Bundesbank's two-week repo move ruffled few feathers. Traders noted the implicit threat but saw little chance of a rate hike while the German economy remained fragile.
New evidence of that came in the shape of a downward-revision to German May industrial production to 99.3 from 100.6. The west German figure was revised to 95.8 from 97.1.
